prompt:
A meteorological balloon of total mass 3.20 kg is released from rest at ground level. A constant upward buoyant force of 45.0 N acts on the balloon. The acceleration of free fall is 9.81 m s^-2.
(a) Calculate the initial upward acceleration of the balloon at the instant of release. [2]
(b) Describe and explain how the upward acceleration and upward velocity of the balloon change as it rises, until it reaches terminal velocity. [2]
hints: Find the weight of the balloon and calculate the initial net upward force.
Consider the direction and speed-dependence of the air resistance opposing the upward motion.
solution:
(a) Weight W = mg = 3.20 kg x 9.81 m s^-2 = 31.392 N.
Initial net force F_net = Upthrust - Weight = 45.0 N - 31.392 N = 13.608 N upwards.
Initial acceleration a = F_net / m = 13.608 N / 3.20 kg = 4.25 m s^-2 upwards.
(b) As the balloon rises and its upward speed increases, the downward air resistance increases. This decreases the resultant upward force, so the upward acceleration decreases. The upward velocity continues to increase but at a decreasing rate, until downward drag plus weight equals the upward buoyant force, at which point acceleration becomes zero and the balloon rises at a constant terminal velocity.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 1: Calculate downward weight W = 3.20 x 9.81 = 31.392 N.
Step 2: At release drag is 0, so F_net = 45.0 - 31.392 = 13.608 N.
Step 3: Initial acceleration a = 13.608 / 3.20 = 4.25 m s^-2.
Step 4: As speed increases upwards, downward drag D increases.
Step 5: Net upward force F_net = Upthrust - W - D decreases, so acceleration decreases.
Step 6: Velocity levels off to a steady terminal velocity when Upthrust = W + D.

mark_scheme.criterion: As upward speed increases, downward air resistance increases, so resultant upward force decreases and acceleration decreases
Upward velocity increases at a decreasing rate until drag plus weight balances upthrust, where acceleration is zero and velocity is constant (terminal velocity)
